name: Beta-glucan

lead: Beta-glucans are sugar polymers from oats, barley, yeast and fungi. In skincare, oat and yeast forms appear in creams and serums to hydrate and soothe, so skin looks calmer, less red and less dry.

Cosmetic descriptions cite water-binding and film-forming properties. Most research concerns other roles: oat beta-glucan is a soluble fibre for which the US FDA approved a heart-disease risk claim in 1997 relating to LDL cholesterol, and immune cells recognise beta-glucans through dectin-1 and related receptors. No clinical trial in the sources reviewed tested topical beta-glucan for appearance.

paras: People use it in soothing creams, serums and masks, often oat or yeast based, applied to dry or irritated skin as part of a calming routine.
Oral forms are widely eaten as fibre. The sources reviewed list no specific topical safety signals, and also provide no topical safety trials.

angle.text: Beta-glucan forms a hydrating film on skin, so it looks calmer, less red and less dry. It is well studied as dietary fibre and an immune trigger, while topical appearance use has not been trialled in the sources reviewed.

lead: Beta-glucans are a family of polysaccharides built from beta-linked glucose units, found in the cell walls of cereals such as oats and barley, yeasts, fungi, algae and some bacteria. Their structure, solubility and biological behaviour vary by source.[1]

In skincare, oat and yeast beta-glucans are marketed as soothing, hydrating ingredients. Outside cosmetics, oat beta-glucan is best known as a soluble fibre for which the US FDA approved a heart-disease risk claim in 1997 relating to LDL cholesterol.[1]

Laboratory immunology has established that beta-glucans are recognised by the immune receptor dectin-1 on macrophages.[2][3] No clinical trial in the sources reviewed has tested topical beta-glucan for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Oats, barley, baker's yeast, mushrooms, algae

paras: Cereal beta-glucans have an unbranched mixed beta-1,3/1,4 backbone and are soluble. Yeast beta-glucans have a beta-1,3 backbone with long beta-1,6 branches and are a common supplement source. Fungal beta-glucans have shorter branches and are insoluble; mushrooms such as shiitake and maitake are under preliminary research for immune effects.[1]

Beta-glucan gums are used as texturing agents in cosmetic and nutraceutical products,[1] and brands market oat and yeast forms for soothing and moisturising. Published human evidence for these skin claims is not found in the sources reviewed.

Oat beta-glucan at around 3 g per day has been associated with lowering LDL cholesterol, and the FDA approved a related coronary-heart-disease claim in 1997. As a fermentable fibre it acts as a prebiotic.[1] A blood assay for (1,3)-beta-D-glucan is also used as an aid in detecting invasive fungal infection.[1]

Dectin-1 was identified in 2001 as a beta-glucan receptor and shown to be the major beta-glucan receptor on macrophages.[2][4] Studies show it works with Toll-like receptor 2 to induce inflammatory responses, and that it is needed for control of fungal infection; people with dectin-1 deficiency have shown mucocutaneous fungal infections.[5][6][7] A 2009 review covered the effects of beta-glucan on human immune and cancer cells.[8]

No studies found on topical beta-glucan for skin appearance in the sources reviewed. Registered human trials examine oral beta-glucan for other outcomes: lipid profile and glycaemia,[9] postprandial blood glucose,[10] immune function in healthy volunteers,[11] and as an add-on in cancer settings.[12]

timeline.event: A report on oat bran lowering cholesterol raised interest in oat beta-glucan.[1]
FDA approved a coronary heart disease claim for oat beta-glucan.[1]
